title: Are the United States and Its Allies Learning Quickly Enough from the War in Ukraine?
gist: Lt. Gen. (Ret.) Curtis Buzzard, former head of SAG-U/NSATU, argues from 30+ trips to Ukraine that the U.S. and its allies are watching the war but not learning fast enough. He points to a drone-driven 'unmanned contact layer' run through the DELTA C2 system, a Russian drone force reportedly doubling to more than 160,000, EW as a core capability, and cost-exchange problems in air defense. He calls for AUTOWARCOM to send a clear procurement demand signal, a U.S.-Ukraine 'drone deal', a larger Test in Ukraine program, and access to battlefield data to train AI and autonomy.

insights.claim: Buzzard argues that watching a war is not the same as learning from it, and that the side that moves through the observe-learn-adapt-fight cycle faster gains the advantage.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense budgets and procurement reform will increasingly favor rapid-iteration vendors over slow, exquisite-platform programs.
insights.quote: Learning velocity is a form of combat power.
insights.locator: The Race to Learn and Adapt

insights.claim: Western procurement, requirements, budgeting cycles and risk management were built for a different era and cannot move at battlefield speed, leaving dangerous gaps between combat needs and what institutions can deliver.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Pressure for acquisition reform is a structural tailwind for defense tech startups and against legacy contracting models.
insights.locator: The West has often struggled

insights.claim: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea are all studying Ukraine's war, including unmanned tactics, LEO network vulnerabilities, Western equipment performance and electronic warfare, so the U.S. risks being out-learned.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Adversary adaptation shortens the useful life of Western capabilities and raises the urgency of defense spending.
insights.locator: And there is a larger strategic concern.

insights.claim: Buzzard says much U.S. learning from Ukraine remains episodic and unevenly institutionalized, despite lessons-learned processes and SAG-U, and that the problem is not too few lessons-learned bodies but no single owner of the whole cycle.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch for organizational changes such as AUTOWARCOM taking ownership of the cycle as signals of real reform.
insights.quote: If nobody owns the cycle from observation through adaptation, the cycle slows down.
insights.locator: The institutional challenge therefore

themes.theme: Unmanned contact layer and the DELTA system

insights.claim: Drones have created an 'air-ground littoral', a persistent contested zone from the ground into low-altitude airspace that enables a highly lethal tactical reconnaissance-strike complex.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Counter-drone systems, low-altitude sensing and small UAS are now central to land warfare, a durable demand theme.
insights.locator: The Unmanned Contact Layer Is Changing

insights.claim: Ukraine's DELTA command and control system has over 200,000 users and lets drone teams share intelligence and run find-fix-finish-exploit-analyze-disseminate (F3EAD) targeting in near real time; Buzzard calls it the 'secret sauce' of Ukrainian unmanned effectiveness.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Software-defined C2 and battlefield networks (cellular, encrypted wireless, LEO satellites, cloud) are where much of the value sits, not only the drone airframes.
insights.quote: DELTA is really the “secret sauce” that makes unmanned systems so effective.
insights.locator: A minimally manned or unmanned contact

insights.claim: Buzzard says drones are not replacing tanks, artillery or aircraft but will change how many are needed and how they are organized; for example, future tanks could carry drones, onboard EW and active protective armor.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Legacy platform makers remain relevant if they integrate unmanned teaming and EW, which points to upgrade and retrofit programs.
insights.quote: Despite pronouncements, drones are not replacing tanks, artillery, or aircraft entirely.
insights.locator: Despite pronouncements, drones are not

insights.claim: Drone innovation continues nonstop in range, speed, payload, frequencies, optics, nascent AI, and fiber-optic control that makes jamming ineffective, and Buzzard says the future of drone warfare will increasingly be about autonomy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Autonomy software and combat-data-trained AI are the next competitive frontier in unmanned systems.
insights.quote: The future of drone warfare will increasingly be about autonomy
insights.locator: A drone may identify a target

themes.theme: Dedicated drone forces: Ukraine USF, Russia, AUTOWARCOM

insights.claim: Ukraine's separate Unmanned Systems Forces, led by Major Robert 'Magyar' Brovdi, a former grain trader and art dealer, command about 12 drone units staffed mostly by tech-minded civilians who measure each engagement's effectiveness almost in real time.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Data-driven performance management of drone crews is a model Western militaries may adopt, creating demand for battlefield analytics.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s Separate Unmanned Systems Forces

insights.claim: Russia is reportedly doubling its unmanned force to over 160,000 personnel in 2026, adding drone companies to battalions, battalions to brigades and regiments to divisions, which would make it larger than most European armies.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Russia's drone scale-up raises European counter-UAS and drone procurement needs; bullish for European defense spending.
insights.quote: This Russian drone force will be larger than most European armies.
insights.locator: Russia appears to have reached

insights.claim: Buzzard recommends a dedicated unmanned systems branch across the U.S. services, with organic drone capability in every formation as well as specialized drone units, and clear command relationships set in peacetime.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Structural force-design change would create a lasting budget line for small UAS, training and counter-UAS.
insights.locator: The effectiveness of all these formations

insights.claim: Buzzard argues the new U.S. Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM) should send a sustained demand signal to industry on quantities, timelines and the mix of attritable, expendable and sophisticated systems, because without credible paths from experimentation to procurement companies will not invest in production capacity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Clear AUTOWARCOM requirements and procurement priorities would be a key catalyst for scaling drone and autonomy makers; watch its first acquisition plans.
insights.quote: companies have little incentive to invest in the facilities, workforce, suppliers, and production capacity required to deliver at scale
insights.locator: AUTOWARCOM should also help create

themes.theme: Electronic warfare central; GPS munitions degraded

insights.claim: Electronic warfare is now central to combat, and new Ukrainian soldiers get more than 30 hours of dedicated training on the electromagnetic spectrum, jamming and direction-finding equipment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: EW and spectrum-management suppliers have a structural tailwind; Buzzard says Western militaries need more EW at all echelons.
insights.locator: Electronic Warfare Is Not a Niche

insights.claim: GPS-aided munitions perform worse in heavily contested electromagnetic environments, and jam-resistant older technologies such as laser-guided munitions are regaining relevance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Demand shifts toward jam-resistant guidance (laser, alternative navigation, autonomy); a risk for GPS-dependent precision munitions programs.
insights.quote: Older technologies, such as laser-guided munitions, can regain relevance because of their resistance to jamming.
insights.locator: This robust electronic warfare environment

insights.claim: More sophisticated EW and air defense are speeding up the need for autonomy in unmanned systems, which must adapt to interference in real time and pass what they learn about enemy jamming and air defenses to later attack waves.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: EW intensity directly drives demand for autonomous swarming and onboard AI.
insights.locator: Lastly, a major implication

themes.theme: Cost exchange, layered air defense, deep strike

insights.claim: Ukraine's indigenous long-range drones ('precision mass') are striking Russian petroleum storage and refining facilities, strategic logistics, defense industrial sites and the shadow fleet, alongside emerging Ukrainian cruise and ballistic missiles.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Continued strikes on Russian refining and the shadow fleet are an ongoing supply risk for Russian refined product exports and a factor in oil and product markets.
insights.locator: In terms of operational depth

insights.claim: Patriot shortages and the growing sophistication of Russian long-range one-way attack drones have pushed Ukraine into a new rapid innovation cycle to build its own interceptors.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Interceptor shortages point to large demand for low-cost interceptors and expanded Patriot production.
insights.quote: Due to shortages in Patriots and the increased sophistication and speed of long-range one-way attack drones
insights.locator: In terms of operational depth

insights.claim: Buzzard argues that defending against massed missiles and drones only with expensive interceptors is unsustainable, so future air defense must layer EW, deception, passive sensing, lower-cost interceptors and guns, and save high-end interceptors for the hardest engagements, which is especially relevant to China in the Indo-Pacific.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Favors makers of low-cost interceptors, gun-based air defense and passive sensors; cost exchange is now a procurement criterion.
insights.quote: Defending against such attacks exclusively with expensive interceptors is unlikely to be sustainable.
insights.locator: This is particularly evident in air

insights.claim: Artillery remains critical, especially when weather grounds drones, but guns 10-15 km behind the front must be mobile and survivable with extended-range munitions, and active-emitting counterfire radars may need passive acoustic or visual cueing.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports extended-range munition and self-propelled artillery demand; radar programs face survivability scrutiny.
insights.locator: The same principle applies to artillery.

insights.claim: Buzzard says sustainment in modern war increasingly includes software, batteries, antennas, spare parts, data, electronic components and industrial capacity to adapt quickly, which changes the definition of logistics.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense supply chains for batteries and electronics become strategic bottlenecks, which matters for component suppliers.
insights.quote: The definition of logistics is changing because the character of the force is changing.
insights.locator: The same is true of sustainment.

insights.claim: Buzzard urges using the war as a filter for every major capability, asking how it would perform in Ukraine today, how the enemy would defeat it, and what it would cost at scale, and asks whether the U.S. is buying for the next war or the last one.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Programs that cannot show combat relevance against EW, drones and an adaptive enemy face budget risk.
insights.quote: Are the United States and its allies buying for the next war—or optimizing for the last one?

themes.theme: Brave1, Test in Ukraine, and combat data

insights.claim: Ukraine's Brave1 defense-tech cluster links the military, industry, investors and developers through grants, codification and its Test in Ukraine program, producing innovation cycles measured in weeks rather than years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Ukraine is a fast validation venue for defense tech; vendors proven there gain credibility.
insights.quote: The result is an innovation cycle measured in weeks rather than years.
insights.locator: The Ecosystem Is the Advantage

insights.claim: Buzzard criticizes Western industry for sometimes delivering capability to Ukraine that is several life cycles behind, and says systems that survive and perform in Ukraine deserve serious consideration for high-end conflict.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Combat validation in Ukraine is becoming a selection criterion that could favor agile entrants over incumbents with outdated offerings.
insights.quote: Industry has sometimes delivered capability to Ukraine that is several life cycles behind, which is embarrassing.
insights.locator: One key point is that capabilities

insights.claim: Buzzard argues Ukraine arguably has the world's most valuable contemporary combat data, already shared under Ukrainian ownership through Avengers AI and the Brave1 Dataroom, and that this data is the key ingredient for military AI and autonomy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Access to combat data is a competitive moat for defense AI companies; watch U.S.-Ukraine data-sharing agreements.
insights.quote: Quite frankly, data is the currency of war, and Ukraine is fighting with “live data.”
insights.locator: Data Is the Currency of War

insights.claim: Buzzard recommends that Washington sign a 'drone deal' with Ukraine, speed up U.S.-Ukraine joint development, coproduction and procurement, expand Test in Ukraine, and set up reciprocal access to battlefield data, building on AUTOWARCOM and Project Meridian.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A U.S.-Ukraine drone deal would be a catalyst for coproduction partnerships between U.S. defense firms and Ukrainian drone makers.
insights.locator: That requires institutionalizing the relationship
